title: Dow Theory
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/0/body: **Dow theory** comes from the ideas of **Charles Dow**, co-founder of The Wall Street Journal in the late 19th century, and others organized it later. Its first principle: **price reflects everything**. News and expectations all show up in price.
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/0/tip: Many of today's technical analysis concepts, like higher highs and higher lows, have their roots in this theory.
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/1/body: In Dow's view, the market has **three kinds of trend** running at the same time: the **primary** trend, the **secondary** trend, which is a correction against the primary one, and the **minor** trend, which is the short day-to-day swings.
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/1/tip: A secondary trend usually retraces one third to two thirds of the primary trend's previous move.
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/2/pairs/0/me: A big move lasting a year or more
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/2/pairs/1/me: A correction lasting weeks to months
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/2/pairs/2/me: A short swing under three weeks
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/2/pairs/3/me: The averages must move the same way
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/3/statement: According to Dow theory, price reflects all available information, including news and market expectations.
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/3/explanatio: That's Dow's first principle: everything the market knows or expects, from news to fear, shows up in price. That's why technical analysts focus on price itself.
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/4/body: Two more key principles: **the averages must confirm each other** (Dow compared the industrial average with the transportation average), and **a trend is assumed to continue until it gives a definite reversal signal**.
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/5/prompt: The industrial average made a new high, but the transportation average couldn't clear its previous high. What does that mean in Dow terms?
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/5/options/0: The uptrend isn't confirmed, so be careful
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/5/options/1: The uptrend has definitely gotten stronger
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/5/options/2: The market will surely crash tomorrow
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/5/options/3: The transportation average doesn't matter at all
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/5/explanatio: Dow's logic: if factories are producing more, transport companies should get busier too. When one doesn't confirm, the trend is in question. But it's a warning, not a sure prediction.
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/6/prompt: In Dow theory, what structure defines an uptrend? Which description fits this chart?
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/6/explanatio: On this chart, each high is above the previous high and each low is above the previous low. That's Dow's definition of an uptrend.
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/7/prompt: Dow says a trend continues until a definite reversal signal. Tap the first candle that closed **below the last higher low (HL)**.
lessons/elliott-u1-l1/steps/7/explanatio: Up to here, the lows kept getting higher. A close below 2930 (the last HL) is the first serious reversal signal; from here, you can't safely assume the uptrend continues.
lessons/elliott-u1-l2/title: The Three Phases of a Trend
lessons/elliott-u1-l2/steps/0/body: Dow said every primary uptrend has three phases: **accumulation**, when smart money quietly buys; **public participation**, when the trend becomes obvious and most traders jump in; and **distribution**, when smart money sells to an excited crowd.
lessons/elliott-u1-l2/steps/1/body: Each phase has a **crowd mood**: **despair** and indifference in accumulation, **confidence** and good news in public participation, and **excitement and greed** in distribution, right when everyone is sure price will keep rising.
lessons/elliott-u1-l2/steps/1/tip: When everyone everywhere is talking about buying an asset, the market may be in the distribution phase.
lessons/elliott-u1-l2/steps/2/prompt: Put the three phases of a Dow uptrend in order.
lessons/elliott-u1-l2/steps/2/explanatio: First smart money buys quietly, then the trend becomes obvious and the crowd piles in, and finally smart money sells to that same crowd.
lessons/elliott-u1-l2/steps/3/prompt: After a long decline, price has been stuck in a narrow range for a while, volume has dried up, and the news is still negative. In Dow terms, which phase are we probably in?
lessons/elliott-u1-l2/steps/3/explanatio: The decline has stopped, price has gone sideways and nobody is interested. That fits the accumulation phase. Still, it's only confirmed when price breaks out of the range to the upside.
lessons/elliott-u1-l2/steps/4/body: The **distribution** phase usually comes after a big rally: price stops making strong new highs and turns into a **range**, while the news is great. Here, smart money slowly sells its positions to newcomers.
lessons/elliott-u1-l2/steps/5/prompt: Tap the candle that marks the start of the **public participation phase**: price's strong breakout from the accumulation range.
lessons/elliott-u1-l2/steps/5/explanatio: After weeks of going nowhere, this big candle closed above the top of the range. From here, the trend is visible to everyone and more traders jump in.
lessons/elliott-u1-l2/steps/6/statement: In the accumulation phase, the news is usually great and everyone is buying with excitement.
lessons/elliott-u1-l2/steps/6/explanatio: That describes distribution. In accumulation, the news is usually bad and the crowd is in despair; only patient, informed buyers quietly step in.
lessons/elliott-u1-l2/steps/7/prompt: A crypto coin has rallied fast for months. Now everyone's talking about it and newcomers are buying with excitement, but price hasn't made a new high in weeks. In Dow terms, which phase does this look like?
lessons/elliott-u1-l2/steps/7/options/3: The start of a fresh uptrend
lessons/elliott-u1-l2/steps/7/explanatio: Crowd excitement after a big rally, combined with price failing to make new highs, are classic signs of distribution. It's a warning, not a sure sell signal.
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/0/body: One of Dow's principles: **volume must confirm the trend**. In a healthy uptrend, volume picks up when price **rises** and drops during **pullbacks**, meaning buyers are more active than sellers.
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/1/body: If price makes a **new high** but volume is **lower** than at the previous high, buyer participation is fading. That counts as a **warning of weakness** for the trend, but it's not a sell signal on its own; Dow took his main signals from **price** itself.
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/2/prompt: What does volume say in this uptrend?
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/2/options/0/: It confirms the trend: volume is higher on rallies
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/2/options/1/: It rejects the trend: volume is higher on pullbacks
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/2/options/2/: Volume has nothing to do with the trend
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/2/options/3/: The market will surely reverse tomorrow
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/2/explanatio: The green candles have high volume and the pullback candles low volume: buyers are behind the move and the pullbacks are weak. That's exactly the volume confirmation Dow talked about.
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/3/prompt: Price has tried twice to break resistance at 2400. Tap the candle that shows a **valid** breakout confirmed by volume.
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/3/explanatio: The first attempt only poked a wick above 2400 and closed below it on low volume. This candle closed with its full body above resistance on much higher volume, so real buyers are behind the break.
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/4/prompt: BTC has been swinging below resistance at 64,000. The last candle closed above resistance on much higher volume than the candles before. Which way is the next move most likely?
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/4/explanatio: A breakout on high volume means real buyer participation; in Dow terms, that confirms the uptrend. Continuation is more likely, though price may pull back to 64,000 first.
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/5/title: Dow in a nutshell for today
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/5/body: Read the trend from **highs and lows**, look for **volume confirmation**, assume the trend continues until a **definite reversal signal**, and remember every primary trend has **secondary corrections**. Elliott was influenced by these same ideas.
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/6/statement: According to Dow, any new high made on lower volume means you should sell right away.
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/6/explanatio: Lower volume is only a warning of weakness. Dow took the reversal signal from price itself, like a break of the last higher low.
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/7/prompt: BTC pulled back in an uptrend, and the pullback candles have much lower volume than the rally candles before them. What does this tell you?
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/7/options/0: The pullback is weak; sellers don't have much strength
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/7/options/1: Sellers have taken full control of the market
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/7/options/2: The primary trend is definitely over
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/7/options/3: Low volume means the market is closed
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/7/explanatio: A pullback on low volume usually means normal profit-taking, not broad selling. That fits with the uptrend continuing.
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/8/sentence: In a healthy uptrend, volume is higher on ___ and lower on ___.
lessons/elliott-u1-l3/steps/8/explanatio: High volume on moves with the trend means real participation; low volume on pullbacks means the other side is weak.
